newsitem.title: USA: Dow snaps 3-session losing streak despite Boeing.
newsitem.headline: Dow snaps 3-session losing streak despite Boeing.

text.p: Wall Street stocks finished higher on Monday, as the Dow industrials overcame a sharp decline in Boeing Co to end their three-session losing streak.

Boeing, a Dow component, slid 6-3/4 to 95-1/4 after the company reported disappointing first-quarter earnings and warned that its shift to newer aircraft models was likely to keep profit margins under pressure for the near term.
The Dow managed to shrug off Boeing's woes, however, gaining 44 points to close unofficially at 6783.

Boeing, which also cited overtime costs and a rapid rise in employment for its lower-than-expected earnings, announced its results at a time when analysts have been on alert for any sign of wage inflation. But such concerns apparently did not hold back the market on Monday.

"It appears no one chose to draw the inference Boeing's problems will translate into the same kinds of problems for other companies," said Michael Metz, chief investment strategist at Oppenheimer & Co.
"That suggests there's still a high degree of confidence in this market," he added.
Interest rate-sensitive stocks, which stand to suffer the most should inflation emerge as a threat, rallied throughout the session.
The gains, which were concentrated among banking shares, surprised some on Wall Street, coming as they did just ahead of a heavy calendar of economic data.
"To some degree, people are placing their bets," said Peter Green, vice president of technical research at Gruntal & Co, "and those bets are interest rate sensitive."
Among banks, Wells Fargo and Co gained 8-5/8 to 259-1/4, and Citicorp rose 3-7/8 to 107-1/4.
Interest rates edged lower, with the yield on the benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury easing two basis points to 7.12 percent in late trading.

Beyond the bank rally, the broad market's performance was cautious and mixed, with gainers edging out losers by a six-to-five margin on lighter-than-average volume of about 400 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

Due before Tuesday's market open is the first-quarter Employment Cost Index (ECI). The index, a closely-watched barometer of wage inflation, is the first of a series of key reports scheduled for release this week.
With data on employment, gross domestic product and manufacturing due later in the week, analysts said the mood was likely to become even more cautious in the next few days.
"We still have a very full plate in front of us," said Dick Stein, vice president at U.S. Clearing Corp. "This is a case where the other team has the ball and the rest of us play defense."
Among individual issues, machine toolmaker Giddings & Lewis Inc jumped 6-47/64 to 20-23/64 after Harnischfeger Industries Inc launched a $19-per-share hostile tender offer for the company.

The jump in Giddings' shares suggested investors felt a higher bid would be forthcoming, but analysts expressed doubt Giddings would receive a better offer. Shares in Harnischfeger fell 3-1/8 to 42-1/4.
Nike Inc fell 2-3/4 to 53-3/8 after Hambrecht & Quist downgraded the company to hold from buy, citing a weak U.S. market for the athletic footwear maker.
McDermott International Inc and its majority-owned J. Ray McDermott unit both failed to open for trading. McDermott said the companies would report larger-than-expected fourth-quarter losses.
McDermott also said it was investigating allegations of wrongdoing by former employees. It did not elaborate on the allegations, saying only that they were unrelated to the forecasted losses.
The S&P 500 index rose 7.59 points to 772.96.
The Nasdaq Composite rose 7.74 points to 1217.03.
((-- Wall Street desk, 212-859-1730))
